Tech Report: Woeful Man Utd have no excuses, Carrick is under big pressure

📅 13 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This was a kick in the midriff for Manchester United.
  • They profited from the first one with Phil Foden sent off after hitting out at Bruno Fernandes – in retaliation – after he was booted in the backside by the United captain who somehow went unpunished.
  • But then City played three quarters of this 199th Manchester derby with just 10 men and came out on top with the inevitable and outstanding Erling Haaland scoring his ninth goal against United to become the top scorer in Premier League meetings between these rivals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This was a kick in the midriff for Manchester United. Not once. But twice. And, then, most painfully, a third time with a dismal, dispiriting defeat.

They profited from the first one with Phil Foden sent off after hitting out at Bruno Fernandes – in retaliation – after he was booted in the backside by the United captain who somehow went unpunished.

But then City played three quarters of this 199th Manchester derby with just 10 men and came out on top with the inevitable and outstanding Erling Haaland scoring his ninth goal against United to become the top scorer in Premier League meetings between these rivals. And that was a far more painful and damaging blow.

Erling Haaland has put Manchester City ahead in the derby after a VAR check ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/V0DCwryhFy.

On a day in which thousands of fans protested, accusing co-owners Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers – with Avram Glazer joining Ratcliffe in attendance – of treating them like “s---”, United unfortunately left a nasty whiff of being just that out on the pitch.

United were frankly, woeful. They lacked belief and imagination and attacking instinct and too many of their players – their apparent big players – went missing when they needed to stand up and take the game by the scruff of the neck. They could not break down City’s defence and failed to be a front-foot team who can dominate the ball. Which is surely what they aspire to be?

According to recent reports, they hit the post twice – through Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo – with efforts from 25 yards. And those two local lads were by far their best players. Without them, United carried so little threat, were so blunt, that it was shocking.

The question for Michael Carrick, the Manchester United head coach, is simple: what is he trying to do with this team? Can they only ever depend on counter-attacks?

According to recent reports, afterwards Haaland talked about City’s “personality, character” and that was exactly what United lacked. They did not adapt a tactical plan to combat 10-man City’s desire to keep their wingers high and wide, and break with intent and still try and attack.

Recent findings suggest that it was telling that so little did City’s new head coach Enzo Maresca worry about United that he did not add a defensive player, and when he took off Rayan Cherki at half-time, he replaced him with the equally creative Iliman Ndiaye who impressed. Maresca knew United needed space to run in behind and denied them that. It was that simple.

City also struck the post with United goalkeeper Senne Lammens tipping an Enzo Fernández shot against the frame of the goal, and the visitors were worthy winners as they preserved their perfect start to the season to draw level on points with leaders, Arsenal.

City handled the occasion and the – admittedly toothless – opposition superbly under their fresh head coach and will clearly be Arsenal’s closest challengers this season.

Recent findings suggest that maresca delivered a masterclass. For Carrick? This was a disasterclass. An object lesson in how not to use a man-advantage. And now United will have to endure even more City songs after being outplayed at home like this.

According to recent reports, was it complacency? Was it inability? Was it a damning lack of courage, confidence, belief even? On the pitch and in the dugout United were far too passive. This was not how a massive team plays and Carrick needs to wake up.

The former midfielder did so well last season to guide United into Champions League qualification but so far this campaign he has given the impression that his job is done. Rather than that the real work starts now.

There was controversy around the red card and the goal. There is no doubt Foden had to go. But what about Fernandes? He clearly kicked Foden as he was on the ground with the midfielder reacting instinctively, two-footing him in the gut.

It meant he became the first City player to be dismissed in a Manchester derby in the league since Bernardo Corradi in December 2006 and will be punished with a three-match ban for violent conduct.

To make matters worse for Foden, who missed out on the World Cup, it happened in front of Thomas Tuchel who names his England squad for the Nations League campaign on Friday.

Phil Foden is SENT OFF in the Manchester derby! 🟥 pic.twitter.com/sDkHoLMnjL.

And the goal? Initially it was ruled out for offside as Haaland superbly turned in Josko Gvardiol’s cross beyond the far post – he made that tricky finish look routine. But after a lengthy VAR check that decision was overturned by referee Michael Oliver.

Industry observers note that patrick Dorgu had played Haaland onside but the issue then was whether Fernández had touched the ball as he tried to reach the cross. He had not. But even if he had not, surely he was impeding Lisandro Martínez’s attempt to clear? He was certainly in the defender’s line of vision which fits the criteria for the offside to be given as it interfered with an opponent.

In a recent development, united can understandably complain but they can have no excuse. The pressure, already, will be beginning to mount on Carrick with just four points from four league games and down in 13th place. With a Carabao Cup tie at home to Brighton in midweek and a trip to Fulham next Sunday before the international break, he needs wins.

“We’ve only got 10 men,” goaded the City fans as the game headed into added time and United can expect to hear that again and again. And again.

Even so, at the death, Bryan Mbeumo – as otherwise anonymous as Matheus Cunha – had the chance to equalise after being shrewdly picked out by Fernandes. He was excellently thwarted by Gianluigi Donnarumma. But Mbeumo was clear inside the penalty area and had to score. Not that United would have deserved it. There were boos at the end and understandably so. United were just not good enough.

Recent findings suggest that I’m confused. We put things in place in the game now. We have people in offices with all the screens for this decision. It’s more worrying about if that’s the interpretation of football now. If that’s the interpretation of not interfering in the game now, that’s really worrying for me. It’s a staggering explanation.

According to recent reports, the decision isn’t going to change the season, but it’s had a major impact on the game. That decision wasn’t on us today. It’s up to us to create and score after that. We had moments. Of course it’s up to us to do that, but substantial moments in games like that have a big impact.

In a recent development, we did a lot of things well, it looked like we were growing well into the game. We looked dangerous. We’ll take the positives from the game today and move on well, but we’re not moving on lightly.

It has been revealed that we could have created more. That’s an answer for us, but we could have. That’s our second defeat now, since I’ve been in charge, but we’re a good team and we’ll get back to wining ways.

The red card changed the blueprint of the game but credit to the players because the effort, spirit and togetherness has been brilliant.

It has been revealed that [On Foden’s red card] Can be a red card, but in the same action can be a red card for Bruno. It is what it is, we won.

Sources indicate that changed the plan for us, and changed the plan for them. They are unbelievable in transition, and the moment we are with 10 men we give them no transitions.

When you are able to win a game with 10 players it’s fantastic, when this game is a derby it’s even better.

We always knew it was going to be a tough game. What happened with Phil at the start wasn’t good for us, but we said at half-time it would make us feel better if we win and we’ve taken three points.

According to recent reports, it just gives you more motivation to go on and get the points. It was really tough for us. We had to run more and fight more. We all shone, to a man, and we were brilliant.

We have to go home with this injustice.

Haaland speaking on Sky: “We had to go low which is not ideal, we like to keep the ball, to try to score goals but in these times you have to go a bit low and take your chances when possible. We managed to do that well and that shows personality and character, to keep the ball away at Old Trafford with 10 men.”.

“We had to change the blueprint a bit, but Enzo gave us a plan where we could play to our different strengths and counter-attack a bit more. For me personally, I just had to be there, to try to wait for a chance, and if there’s a chance, I had to be ready to execute. We also needed fighters in the team, which we have plenty of. Look at our midfield - it’s something they like to do! I’m so, so proud of everyone.”.

And on Donnarumma’s late save: “This wolf in goal giving you so much confidence, he looks a bit like a wolf. He is a mad man but he is a match-winner as well.”.

City win the Old Trafford derby with 10 men and Enzo Maresca runs down the touchline to celebrate in front of the travelling fans while their players embrace Donnarumma after his late save.

There will be so much analysis of Foden’s red card, but more so how Haaland’s winner stood given the final result. Should Enzo Fernandez have been considered offside?

Sources indicate that but if you are judging performances, City are worthy winners. They defended stoutly, carried a threat and kept the ball well for periods even though they were a man light. United were aimless and froze.

A mammoth victory, and one which perhaps puts the breaks on talk of an Arsenal procession.

What a chance for Mbeumo to equalise! Superb save by Donnarumma, after the United forward was found by a Bruno Fernandes disguised pass into the box. Mbeumo took the ball under his spell and shot with power, but the big goalkeeper pushed the shot over the bar.

United have a corner, but Michael Oliver blows for a foul, and that is surely that.

Sources indicate that martinez tries a straight ball towards Sesko, which is too high for the striker. United have perhaps just one more attack in them if they are too salvage a point.

Dorgu with another foul on Ndiaye, yet another break in play for City. And there are going to just FIVE minutes of added time, much to Old Trafford’s frustration.

In a recent development, haaland does well to bring City forward after another United attack breaks down, and Dorgu is penalised for a foul on Ndiaye. Another stoppage follows because the ball hits Michael Oliver. City can see the finish line so, and they would deserve their three points.

Sources indicate that united have a corner after Guehi stands firm to block Cunha’s strike from distance. Maguire rises highest in the middle, but no United player gambled on the knockdown and his header drifts wide of the post.

Good work from Anderson against Mainoo in midfield, he receives a big cheer from the City fans. Carrick has thrown attackers on, but United have lost some structure and are not sustaining pressure.

Nico O’Reilly is now on for the closing stages, in place of Fernandez and Carrick has thrown on Zirkzee in place of Marcus Rashford. A United goal now would feel like a goal out of nowhere. City are playing the better football now and they have a corner.

United have lost all sense of momentum, City are keeping the ball for spells and then are happy for the game to be broken up stoppages.

Fernandez goes down looking for a penalty rather hopefully, and Maguire has been booked for his reaction as well as Fernandez for his role in the fracas. More and more time ticks away.

City are showing real resolve as well as quality here, Enzo Fernandez has just won a free-kick in the United half after a foul by Mainoo. The closest United have come in recent minutes was a glancing header wide from Mbeumo.

From that free-kick, Fernandez’s low delivery is close to being converted by Haaland or Guehi.

It’s a massive final 16 minutes here plus injuries for United. You’re at home to your derby rivals who have been down to 10 men since the 23rd minute and you’ve had just two players show up for the mostpart so far - Mainoo and Rashford. The rest are really going to have to lift it.

This fixture has often brought out the best in Phil Foden but this is a third successive visit to Old Trafford he will want to forget. He was substituted at half-time of the 2-0 defeat in January with a broken hand and the season before he had been withdrawn before the hour mark after a poor performance in a 0-0 draw. And now sent off after 24 minutes.

A half that will be remembered for one thing and one thing only: Phil Foden’s red card for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes.

According to recent reports, united were shading things before that flashpoint, but City will be pleased with their response to the sending off. They have defended well, and posed a threat going forward without executing the final pass or shot.

Thousands of Manchester United fans have been marching in protest at the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s running of the club.

Supporters have reacted with outrage to the club’s handling of a controversial anti ticket touting operation they felt unfairly singled out innocent fans.

And thousands have taken to the streets to voice their anger at how they feel they are being treated by the co-owners.

Plumes of red and green and yellow smoke filled the air as fans brandished banners and flags and chanted anti-Glazer and Ratcliffe songs.

“You take it all from fans and banning us for nothing. Premium prices all for greed,” read one banner.

AC Milan and Adidas will be back together again from 2028, and the German brand want to launch the new era with a bi bang.

According to recent reports, as Calciomercato.com write, Milan will return to being an Adidas club again, as they have been for three previous spells. The two brands became so closely linked above all by the successes of the 2000s under Carlo Ancelotti, before PUMA took over in 2018.

Recent findings suggest that the contract with Adidas – which will begin in the summer of 2028 – is quite a sensational deal for the industry and for the club’s final years in terms of sporting results. It will bring in €50m per season for 10 seasons, the highest in Serie A by some margin.

Ten years ago, the Rossoneri signed a €14m per season contract with PUMA, which was renewed in 2022 to reach around €25m per season.

Adidas have already invested heavily in Milan and they want to strengthen the ‘alliance’ further. A lot depends on building a squad capable of playing a leading role in both Serie A and the Champions League.

Industry observers note that for this reason, Adidas are hoping to help Milan land a world-class player. Napoli midfielder Scott McTominay could gain momentum in the coming months as an idea, as the former Manchester United player is one of Adidas’s most vital players worldwide.

Bruno Fernandes is another name to keep an eye on. The Manchester United captain left Italy many years ago as a promising youngster and now wants to return as a top player. The Portuguese is a possible candidate, even if he is presently twinned with Nike.

Sources indicate that last but not least – in terms of consideration and feasibility – is Real Madrid’s Endrick. Milan are ready to make him one of the symbols of their fresh project and have a bid of €60m plus bonuses ready to try to break down Los Blancos’ wall.

Jose Mourinho is the main obstacle between the Rossoneri and the Brazilian star, but Cardinale is unwavering and ready to do everything possible to bring him to Milanello as early as January. The money from Adidas could help land Endrick, who is with Latest Balance at present.

  • Crystal Palace winger Ismaila Sarr has confirmed that he is in discussions over a newly introduced contract at Selhurst Park after putting Liverpool's summer transfer interest behind him.
  • The 28-year-old Senegal international was keen on a switch to Anfield before the Eagles reportedly rejected a £50m offer from the Merseyside giants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 22 Nov 2026 03:18, Last updated: 22 Nov 2026 03:18.

Crystal Palace winger Ismaila Sarr has confirmed that he is in discussions over a newly introduced contract at Selhurst Park after putting Liverpool's summer transfer interest behind him.

The 28-year-old Senegal international was keen on a switch to Anfield before the Eagles reportedly rejected a £50m offer from the Merseyside giants.

Liverpool had been assessing alternatives to primary target Bradley Barcola before eventually meeting Paris Saint-Germain's £123m asking price.

Despite the frustration of seeing a high-profile move collapse, Sarr insists he remains settled in South London and is open to agreeing improved terms on his current deal that runs until 2029.

Speaking to BBC Sport, the former Watford attacker admitted he naturally gave serious thought to what joining one of world football's biggest clubs would mean for his career.

However, Sarr stressed that he is no longer dwelling on the past and is solely focused on returning from a groin injury that has restricted him to just two Premier League substitute appearances this term.

"Today, that chapter is behind me," Sarr mentioned. "I've always believed that you can't move forward if you're constantly looking in the rear-view mirror.".

Recent findings suggest that addressing his long-term future with the club, the winger confirmed: "Yes, there have been discussions with the club. For now, I prefer to let those conversations happen privately and concentrate on football.".

Sarr netted 21 goals across all competitions last season to help Palace lift the Conference League trophy and the board are keen to reward his stature in the squad.

When Sarr completes his recovery, he will return to work under latest head coach Thomas Frank following the dismissal of Pierre Sage.

The former Brentford and Tottenham Hotspur manager endured a chastening start to his tenure on Saturday as a late Dwight McNeil own goal condemned Palace to a 3-2 defeat at Coventry City.

That setback stretched the Eagles' dismal run to five consecutive Premier League losses, leaving them mired in an unexpected early relegation battle.

Nevertheless, Sarr remains adamant that the dressing room possesses the quality and collective resilience required to spark a turnaround under Frank's fresh approach.

"We all have to take responsibility, work together and fight for every point," Sarr added. "I'm confident we can overcome this difficult period and achieve our objectives this season.".

Palace host Real Sociedad in the Europa League on Thursday before welcoming Hull City to Selhurst Park for Frank's home bow in charge of the Eagles.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • Recent findings suggest that some grounds are beautiful.
  • But each of them holds the soul of their community and the hopes and dreams of the thousands of people who make the pilgrimage there every weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026.

Recent findings suggest that some grounds are beautiful. Some grounds are not so beautiful. Some grounds take you to the heart of the English game. And some leave you feeling like you're on the periphery.

But each of them holds the soul of their community and the hopes and dreams of the thousands of people who make the pilgrimage there every weekend.

On April 1, 2025, I made the trip to Harrogate Town’s Exercise Stadium and first fulfilled the quest of a lifetime by completing the set of all 92 English Football League grounds for Daily Mail Sport. But then Everton moved away from Goodison Park and into a stunning newly introduced stadium on the banks of the River Mersey.

I was one short again but on February 23, 2026, I got back up to 92 by going to Hill Dickinson Stadium to watch Everton versus Manchester United. Then, in November, with York City being promoted (alongside Rochdale, whose ground I had ticked off decades ago), I made the trip to the LNER Stadium to make the 92 whole again.

Sources indicate that I won’t give too much away just yet, but why are grounds like AFC Wimbledon and Exeter City in my top 20? What about Anfield, Old Trafford and Stamford Bridge? Where does Everton’s dazzling new home rank? Where is the best grub in the Premier League and where did Tyson Fury once threaten to have my jaw broken?

In a recent development, this is my love letter to English football. Read on to find out who comes out on top, where your team ranks and everything else in between – then let me know what you think of my guide to the 92 grounds of England.

Division: Championship Opened: 1993 Capacity: 19,369.

Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir.

According to recent reports, I’ve been banned from The Den for the last 20 months, in a professional capacity anyway. I could still go in a personal capacity but, on balance, I think I’d rather not.

The Daily Mail has been told that our reporters are not welcome at the club because we had the temerity to report on the horrendous challenge by Millwall goalkeeper Liam Roberts on Crystal Palace’s Jean-Philippe Mateta during the FA Cup tie at Selhurst Park in March last year, which left the French striker requiring 25 stitches in his left ear.

In a recent development, let’s be honest about this: there are worse places to be banned from. Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir. You don’t have to be a racist, misogynistic, homophobic bloke with anger issues and a penchant for tragedy-chanting to feel at home at The Den. But it helps.

And, yes, I know Millwall are trying to rebrand themselves as a ‘family club’ now and the odd Tarquin and Tabitha stray across the county lines from Blackheath and Clapham to keep it real but that just makes The Den experience even worse.

The last time I went as a supporter was 16 years ago to watch Stockport County play there and the walk from South Bermondsey station to the away turnstiles was an eye-opener.

In a recent development, not that there were any problems: even at Millwall, football has moved on since the 70s. But this still felt deeply dystopian: for their own safety, away fans walk to the ground through a long wire mesh cage that seems to have no end. It felt like embarking on a tour of Jurassic Park: you know that if the fences fail, the dinosaurs are going to take a run at you.

Inside the ground, which is modern and neat and relatively characterless, the level of hatred for visiting supporters feels unusually visceral. It’s loud. I’ll give it that. It’s primeval. It’s unreconstructed, which can be a good thing, too, and it breeds a sense of togetherness.

Recent findings suggest that if medievalism is your thing, you’re in for a treat. If not, give it a miss.

Division: League One Opened: 2007 Capacity: 30,303.

I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons, for that matter.

I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons themselves for that matter.

The club was born under a bad sign when it was jemmied out of Wimbledon and moved to Milton Keynes in 2003 and it has never been able to shake the stigma since. The stadium fits the club.

It has been revealed that it is a soulless, faceless, gloomy place. More than that, there is something rather forbidding about it. Its 30,000 capacity is too significant for the club it hosts and, apart from the joys of the local KFC and McDonald’s, there is little to recommend in its immediate surrounds. Its black seats lend it a sinister air, too.

It’s the kind of stadium only its mother could love. And it doesn’t have a mother. Unless you want to do the 92, give it a miss.

According to recent reports, 90. Kassam Stadium, Oxford United.

Division: League One Opened: 2001 Capacity: 12,537.

The empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate.

I feel ashamed to say it, given that it is my local club, but the best experience I’ve had at the Kassam Stadium was getting my Covid jab there during the pandemic.

When they moved, around the turn of the century, abandoning the chaotic charm of the Manor Ground in Headington and swapping it for an isolated plateau outside the city, they only completed three sides, abandoning the fourth because of rising costs.

A particularly bitter wind blows in off the car park behind one of the goals and, from the main stand – in fact, from every stand – there is a magnificent and uninterrupted view of the Frankie and Benny's in the mini retail park that abuts the ground.

The empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, too, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate given they have endured a generation of being stuck here. Firoz Kassam still owns the stadium but not the club. That kind of separation always spells trouble.

It has been revealed that oxford are hoping to move to a newly introduced stadium to the north of the city in a couple of years’ time. It can’t come soon enough.

It has been revealed that 89. London Stadium, West Ham United.

Division: Championship Opened: 2012 Capacity: 62,500.

It was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground.

In a recent development, I don’t even like calling it the London Stadium. It’s the Olympic Stadium, but it suited the David Sullivan-Karren Brady rebrand of the club to give it the capital’s name.

According to recent reports, it was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground. It’s also a monument to much that is wrong with the upper reaches of the English game: a surrender of identity and tradition as collateral damage in the owners’ pursuit of profit.

According to recent reports, walking to it, sadly, feels a bit like walking through a wasteland and its odd configuration inside harms the atmosphere even though the fans are right up there with the best in the country. The old stadium at Upton Park was intimate and raucous and intimidating. The London Stadium is nothing like that.

The owners spent a lot of time congratulating themselves on the deal they did to move to the new ground: they’re the archetypes of football owners who know the price of everything and the value of nothing.

88. Hillsborough, Sheffield Wednesday.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 34,835.

It is hard to get past Hillsborough's association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and the betrayal of supporters.

I used to think of Hillsborough as one of the cathedrals of the English game but since the disaster that claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool fans in 1989, it is hard to get past its association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and betrayal of supporters.

I know, obviously, that this would punish Wednesday fans who do not deserve to be punished for something that had nothing to do with them but Hillsborough, and its Leppings Lane End in particular, has such a cursed legacy that part of me thinks it should have been demolished and that the club should have moved elsewhere.

Even in the last couple of years, fans of Newcastle United and Leeds United have reported serious safety concerns in the Leppings Lane End.

I recognise the flaws in my argument about demolishing the stadium, or part of it, and the emotions it provokes on all sides so perhaps it’s just enough to say I’ll never feel the same about the stadium as I once did.

Visiting it now feels like an intrusion.

It has been revealed that 87. Sixfields, Northampton Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1994 Capacity: 8,203.

Sixfields is a soulless ground anyway but its issues have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

Sixfields is a blighted stadium.

It is a soulless ground anyway but its issues have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

Sources indicate that it has the same kind of deracinated feel as so many of the new-build stadia pushed to the peripheries of towns. Its supporters deserve a lot better.

86. Broadfield Stadium, Crawley Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1997 Capacity: 5,907.

If you visit the Broadfield Stadium, I think you might doubt if Crawley are even in League Two.

Not an awful lot to relish about the Broadfield Stadium, to be honest.

Decent fans, of course, just like at every club, but Crawley Town’s home is a bit of a modern monstrosity, next to a roundabout outside town on the A23.

Sources indicate that if you visit the Broadfield Stadium, I think you might doubt if Crawley are even in League Two. I had fun when I visited because I was in the away end with Stockport fans but I’m not in any hurry to go back.

Industry observers note that 85. Coventry Building Society Arena, Coventry City.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2005 Capacity: 32,609.

Football at the CBS Arena feels like it is in an urban wasteland but it is football, nonetheless.

When it was called the Ricoh Arena, I had no interest in visiting what is now the Coventry Building Society Arena because it felt like a symbol of the callous way in which fans of the club were being treated by SISU, the hedge fund that owned it at the time.

Sources indicate that but SISU sold up in the end and I went along a few years back to see Coventry dismantle Wayne Rooney’s Birmingham City. Then, in the press room beneath the stadium, I watched as my colleague Neil Moxley got into a decent old-fashioned row with Rooney about his stewardship of the Blues.

The atmosphere inside the ground was lively enough, partly because the game was a derby of sorts, but it is a soulless stadium abutting the M6.

It is football in an urban wasteland but it is football, nonetheless, and Doug King, the new owner, has brought with him much better times.

Recent findings suggest that 84. JobServe Community Stadium, Colchester United.

Division: League Two Opened: 2008 Capacity: 10,105.

This stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is rather a bleak place to watch football.

The staff at the club are great, the stewards are friendly, there's plenty of parking, there's a Wendy's next door and the home fans, largely arranged in a stand behind one of the goals, make a superb first of creating an atmosphere.

But this stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is still rather a bleak place to watch football.

It probably didn’t help that I went on a dank March night when a wispy fog lingered in the dim floodlight glare but there was something ethereally gloomy about the JobServe Community Stadium.

Industry observers note that the empty corridors and the cavernous suites lent it a slight feel of the Overlook Hotel on the inside. On the outside, the four corners of the stadium are open, which makes for especially bitter nights in the winter.

Home is home and there was still plenty of drama and passion in Colchester’s 1-0 victory over Chesterfield – the match I saw – but it came despite the stadium, not because of it.

83. Pallet-Track Bescot Stadium, Walsall.

Division: League Two Opened: 1990 Capacity: 10,863.

The Bescot Stadium was the first of the generation of identikit upcoming-build arenas I went to and there is not, frankly, much to recommend it apart from the loyalty of the fans.

The Bescot was the first of the generation of identikit new-build arenas I went to and there is not, frankly, much to recommend it apart from the loyalty of the fans.

It’s close to the M6 and it’s a seven-minute walk to Walsall station – so you can get away from it swiftly, which some would say is a bonus.

82. Brick Community Stadium, Wigan Athletic.

Division: League One Opened: 1999 Capacity: 25,133.

The name changes are irrelevant to some but they betray a lack of care for the identity of a football club.

I stood on the terraces at Springfield Park as a Stockport fan.

Once again, it will not come as a surprise to learn I preferred it to its successor, the JJB Stadium, which later became the DW Stadium and is now the Brick Community Stadium.

The name changes are irrelevant to some but they betray a lack of care for the identity of a football club.

There were some great days and nights there when Wigan were promoted to the Premier League and I remember, in particular, the heady feeling of watching Wigan’s first home game in the top flight, against Jose Mourinho’s Chelsea in 2005.

The limelight has moved away again now and Wigan are left with a stadium that is perfectly adequate and also perfectly unremarkable.

It has been revealed that 81. The Croud Meadow, Shrewsbury Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 2007 Capacity: 9,875.

Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

Gay Meadow, the former home of Shrewsbury Town, was one of the best grounds in our top four divisions.

It might have flooded now and again because of its position on the banks of the River Severn but it was a fine old ground and the tradition of a boatman taking to a coracle to fish wayward shots that cleared the roof of the stand out of the river was one of the most cherished peculiarities in our game.

According to recent reports, the Croud Meadow is altogether more prosaic. Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

Industry observers note that 80. Select Car Leasing Stadium, Reading.

Division: League One Opened: 1998 Capacity: 24,376.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006, when Steve Coppell and Wally Downes were in charge at the Madejski Stadium.

People called it the Mad Stad back then and I remember Neil Warnock telling me about being chased to his car outside the main entrance when he was manager of Sheffield United.

And Wally took a swing at me at a Football Writers’ Association dinner a couple of years later.

Anyway, I’ve made up with Stephen Hunt, who was one of the players involved in the tumult against Chelsea, and with Downes since then.

Even if the Mad Stad doesn’t have an awful lot of personality, I have only respect for the Reading fans who endured so much under the ownership of Dai Yongge and fought for their club.

79. Pride Park Stadium, Derby County.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 32,956.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost character because the fans just merge into one.

Pride Park is the standard-bearer, sadly, for what is lacking in many of the new generation of English football stadia.

English football grounds should be about the North Bank and the Stretford End and the Kop and the Gallowgate End and the Shelf.

They’re supposed to be about defined areas that give a stadium character and personality and even rivalry among home fans about who sings loudest.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost that character because the fans just merge into one.

Industry observers note that this is not a criticism of Derby County fans in any way. They still make plenty of noise inside their stadium but the place is not a patch on the Baseball Ground, which witnessed so many momentous days and nights.

Pride Park is bland and featureless, a symbol of its team’s current struggle for identity as it languishes near the foot of the Championship.

78. Swansea.com Stadium, Swansea City.

Division: Championship Opened: 2003 Capacity: 20,996.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks character but is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

My in-laws used to live in Swansea and when I wasn’t out walking to Worm’s Head at Rhossili or enjoying the delights of Mumbles and the Wales Coast Path, I’d make the occasional pilgrimage to what was left of the Vetch Field.

I stood in the away end there with Manchester United fans in the early 80s but when I visited later in my life, the Vetch was locked up and derelict. If you peered through the gates, you could see small trees and shrubs growing on the pitch.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks the same character, obviously, but it is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

It has been revealed that I did a phone interview with Mike Tyson from the press box here a couple of hours before a game once. I couldn’t hear him very well because of various announcements being made over the loud-speaker system and soon, his tone became rather impatient but still, a conversation with Mike Tyson in the press box at Swansea is not easily forgotten.

77. Pirelli Stadium, Burton Albion.

Division: League One Opened: 2005 Capacity: 7,088.

Burton’s a fine club with a distinguished non-League history that can boast Neil Warnock and Nigel Clough as former managers and which has nailed down its place in the Football League.

The main entrance of the Pirelli Stadium looks a little like a car showroom. The rest of it struggles for character, too.

Burton’s a fine club with a distinguished non-League history that can boast Neil Warnock and Nigel Clough as former managers and which has nailed down its place in the Football League.

It has been a club to be admired for a long time, particularly under the former stewardship of Ben Robinson, who sold his majority stake to the Nordic Football Group.

They have punched above their weight for much of that time and their stadium is built for practicality, not for artistic merit.

76. Vitality Stadium, Bournemouth.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1910 Capacity: 11,307.

It’s a bit of a Lego arena, sure, but it’s built for its audience and its catchment area. It’s a League Two stadium that got overtaken by the success of its side.

The club is one of the success stories of modern English football and the Vitality Stadium reflects its enthusiasm and, yes, vitality.

It has been revealed that it’s a bit of a Lego arena, sure, but it’s built for its audience and its catchment area. It’s a League Two stadium that got overtaken by the success of its side.

Its character comes from its small size and the atmosphere it generates because of it.

Abutting King’s Park and not far from the sea front, it’s a ground that almost manages to feel quaint. But not quite.

75. Club Doncaster Sports Village, Doncaster Rovers.

Division: League One Opened: 2007 Capacity: 15,148.

This is a uniform modern bowl on the outside of town rescued by the club’s excellent support.

It is, at least, a pleasant walk to the stadium on the outskirts of Doncaster.

Recent findings suggest that I parked on the estate grouped around Lakeside Lake and strolled around its shores until I came to the stadium. Things go slightly downhill from there.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a perfectly presentable stadium but there is little to distinguish it. It is a uniform modern bowl stuck on the outside of town that is rescued by the club’s excellent support.

74. St Mary's Stadium, Southampton.

Division: Championship Opened: 2001 Capacity: 32,384.

It doesn’t feel as though Southampton's St Mary’s Stadium has any quirks, unfortunately.

Squatting at the edge of a slightly murky industrial estate, it falls squarely into the category of fresh-builds largely devoid of character.

Southampton’s former ground, The Dell, was a wonderfully quirky stadium, full of odd tiers and shelves.

It doesn’t feel as though St Mary’s Stadium has any quirks, unfortunately.

Squatting at the edge of a slightly murky industrial estate, it falls squarely into the category of fresh-builds largely devoid of character.

That does not mean that the home fans are incapable of creating atmosphere there and the renditions of When the Saints Go Marching In are a part of the cultural fabric of football in this country.

Sight lines are good and it can get loud but its design has little to recommend it.

73. King Power Stadium, Leicester City.

Division: League One Opened: 2002 Capacity: 32,259.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans can make plenty of noise but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the new era of stadia.

One of the few times I was genuinely scared at a football stadium when I was a supporter was during a visit to Leicester City’s former stadium at Filbert Street.

In the crush to get out of the away end at the final whistle, I was lifted off my feet in the surge.

So I’m aware that there are limits to how much one should mourn the passing of that generation of stadia but I still find it hard to warm to arenas like the King Power.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans made plenty of noise in happier times but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the fresh generation of stadia.

Even then, it provided me with one of the great memories of the last decade when Andrea Bocelli stood next to Claudio Ranieri and sang Nessun Dorma the game after Leicester had pulled off the shock of the century by winning the Premier League in 2016.

Division: League One Opened: 1961 Capacity: 7,426.

Broadhall Way is a decent little ground with a good atmosphere, and home to a friendly club.

Broadhall Way, now known as the SPORTA Arena, is a decent little ground with a good atmosphere.

And it is home to a fine club, one that has consistently achieved more than most expected of it and has held down its place in the Football League.

The Stevenage fans create more than their share of noise but it’s a friendly club with great staff and stewards.

It’s not spectacular but it’s a lovely day out watching football.

Industry observers note that 71. EV Charger Points Stadium, Cheltenham Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1927 Capacity: 6,923.

EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

It is a high bar in these days when money counts a lot more than heritage and finances are fraught at the wrong end of the EFL, but the EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

We should just stick with Whaddon Road really but it was renamed the Abbey Business Stadium in 2009, then it became The World of Smile Stadium, then the LCI Rail Stadium in 2016–17, then the Jonny-Rocks Stadium in 2018–19, and the Completely-Suzuki Stadium in 2022 and now its current glorious and evocative name.

I hope they got a lot of money for those sponsorships because they make the club look stupid and cheap and rip chunks of its identity away from it.

Industry observers note that again, I know it’s probably not financially viable to do away with them but I hate stadium naming rights. I’d ban them if I could. Football survived for a century without them, so why not now?

It’s a shame because it’s a fine little ground that provides a different focus in a town dominated by horse racing.

In a recent development, 70. LNER Community Stadium, York City.

Division: League Two Opened: 2021 Capacity: 8,500.

Industry observers note that david 'Bumble' Lloyd, England's former cricket coach and a broadcasting legend, is a season-ticket holder at York City. 'A grand stadium,' he stated of the ground the club moved to in January 2021 after 90 years at Bootham Crescent.

After York's promotion from the National League last season, it was the only ground of the 92 that I had not visited and I made my first trip there this month for the FA Cup first-round tie against Northampton Town.

The fresh stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

In a recent development, I don't particularly warm to out-of-town stadiums built next to retail parks but York challenged that perception. Society is changing and town planning is changing. Retail parks are our fresh high streets and if a club is to be at the heart of a community, there are worse places for it to be than beside a Hotel Chocolat, an M&S Foodhall, a multiplex cinema, a teaching hospital, a leisure centre and a bowling alley.

I'd paid my homage to Bootham Crescent earlier by visiting the housing estate where it once stood. A small part of the main stand and the players' tunnel has been preserved, which is, at least, a nod to the club's heritage but I wish there were more.

The fresh stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two of the four stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

Sources indicate that their crowds are still excellent and I got to witness the fastest goal I've ever seen, too. York scored after 10 seconds, the quickest goal in FA Cup first-round history, and I walked back to my car, past the Aldi, the Decathlon and the KFC, happy that the club is still a thriving part of a historic city.

69. Priestfield Stadium, Gillingham.

Division: League Two Opened: 1893 Capacity: 11,582.

Some may damn Priestfield but Gillingham have played here for more than 100 years and that weight of history counts as much as anything when you visit a stadium.

I remember the journey as much as anything. Kent might be the county I’ve been to least and so it felt slightly exotic driving down the M2 and seeing the Priestfield Stadium not far from the River Medway.

Some may damn Priestfield but Gillingham have played here for more than 100 years and that weight of history counts as much as anything when you visit a stadium.

However hard clubs may try to replicate tradition with forced rituals, you can’t cheat history.

Recent findings suggest that 68. Copperjax Community Stadium, Bromley.

Division: League One Opened: 1938 Capacity: 5,000.

Sources indicate that hayes Lane is one of those stadiums that feels wide open to the elements. It’s still a pleasure to visit.

It has been revealed that hayes Lane – or the Copperjax Community Stadium, to give it its current name – is one of those stadiums that feels wide open to the elements. It’s the opposite of a tight, enclosed ground like Queens Park Rangers' Loftus Road but it’s still a pleasure to visit.

I went with Stockport when Bromley were in the National League and stood on the open terrace, which was reserved for away fans.

It was a wild evening in February 2022 and it felt as if the wind was blowing horizontal but County won 3-1 and a steward went out of his way to bring me a programme from where they were being sold in the home end, so it felt like a golden night all round.

Division: League Two Opened: 1978 Capacity: 5,032.

Many dislike and distrust the way Gary Neville, Ryan Giggs and the rest took over a non-League club and oversaw its rise to the Football League but I like what they’ve done at Salford.

The players who comprise the Class of 92 were the players at the heart of one of the greatest stories I ever covered – the Manchester United Treble of 1998-99 – so perhaps it shouldn’t be a surprise that I enjoyed my visit to Moor Lane, now rebranded as the AIG Stadium.

Many dislike and distrust the way Gary Neville, Ryan Giggs and the rest took over a non-League club and oversaw its rise to the Football League but I like what they’ve done at Salford.

It’s a neat little ground and it’s been nicely modernised without losing all its character.

Sources indicate that I went to a League Two play-off semi-final there a couple of years ago when Salford played Stockport and the atmosphere was excellent. Stockport lost the first leg but made the final. So that helped.

It has been revealed that 66. One Call Stadium, Mansfield Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1861 Capacity: 9,376.

I didn’t know back when I first went that Field Mill was, and is, the oldest stadium in the league.

My only visit to Field Mill – now the One Call Stadium – was on Saturday, November 20, 1982.

I know this because I have always been a football stadium nerd and my 16-year-old self logged all the matches I went to in a King’s School Macclesfield exercise book.

I didn’t know then that Field Mill was, and is, the oldest continually used stadium in the league but I stood on an open terrace behind one of the goals that housed the away fans and watched Stockport lose 3-2 in an FA Cup first-round tie.

Sources indicate that maybe that was why I’ve never been back. The atmosphere was a little bit lost because it seemed so open but there is a stand now where that open terrace was. So maybe things have improved.

Division: Championship Opened: 1921 Capacity: 22,200.

I’ve always associated Watford's home at Vicarage Road with drama for some reason.

I’m going to show my age again: the first time I went to Vicarage Road, Graham Taylor was the manager, in his first spell at the club, and Ross Jenkins was playing up front in a match against Manchester United.

Maybe I’ve misremembered this but I seem to recall the train dropping us away fans right outside the stadium.

I’ve always associated Vicarage Road with drama for some reason. Even though it’s not tight and compact, it’s a place that can still generate a terrific atmosphere and I’ve seen a slew of upsets there.

The last one was when Liverpool visited in the middle of their runaway title-winning season in 2019-20.

Recent findings suggest that they were still unbeaten in mid-February and on a long winning run and Watford took them apart and beat them 3-0. It was the kind of occasion that Vicarage Road excels at.

64. Riverside Stadium, Middlesbrough.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 33,931.

It is a friendly, passionate place to watch a game but its design is unimaginative and bland.

The location of the Riverside Stadium on the banks of the Tees, set against the backdrop of the region’s industrial heritage in steel and chemicals, makes it feel as if the stadium is at the heart of its community.

Everton’s latest ground is the latest to use its city’s waterway as a backdrop but the drawback to Middlesbrough’s home is its featureless interior.

It is a friendly, passionate place to watch a game but its design is unimaginative and bland.

The bitter wind blowing in from the North Sea can make the walk to the stadium a challenge for the efficacy of your winter clothes, too.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 30,089.

Even if their latest ground lacks character in its architecture, Stoke fans have breathed life into it with their raucous vitality.

There was a time, when Tony Pulis was manager of Stoke City, that a visit to the bet365 Stadium was regarded as the ultimate test of fortitude.

That was when the Sky pundit Andy Gray suggested Lionel Messi ‘would struggle on a cold night at the Britannia Stadium’, the ground’s former name.

Recent findings suggest that A visit to the stadium is a test for fans, too. It generates a decent atmosphere but the design of it means the wind blows through the gaps between the stands and chills supporters to the bone on cold days and nights.

A little way away, on the other side of the dual carriageway that runs down towards the M6, you used to be able to see the contours of the Victoria Ground, the club’s former home, etched into the patch of wasteland where it once stood but they have built a housing estate on it now.

Even if their latest ground lacks character in its architecture, the fans have breathed life into it with their raucous vitality.

62. Blundell Park, Grimsby Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1899 Capacity: 9,052.

According to recent reports, ground experiences are about a lot more than the game. They’re about going with your mates, getting a sense of the local community, embedding yourself in tradition and the game, too.

I’m not saying that Steel's Cornerhouse fish and chip restaurant is the best thing about Cleethorpes but eating fish fresh from the North Sea certainly made my visit to Blundell Park more memorable.

Ground experiences are about a lot more than the game.

They’re about going with your mates, they’re about getting a sense of the local community, they’re about embedding yourself in tradition and they’re about the game, too.

I loved Blundell Park for all those reasons.

61. Cardiff City Stadium, Cardiff City.

Division: Championship Opened: 2009 Capacity: 33,280.

Cardiff's stadium may not be Ninian Park but it's still a good place to watch football because they are such a passionate group of supporters.

I was a journalism student in Cardiff so Ninian Park was the first ground where I ever sat in a press box. From that day to this, it’s never lost the thrill.

Rob Phillips, Cardiff’s South Wales Echo reporter at the time, was still commentating for the BBC until a few seasons ago. He was the first example I came across of a journalist who was courageous enough to tell the truth even if it meant being banned by his local club. That fate befell him for a spell during my year in Wales.

Anyway, Ninian Park was a force of nature stadium and its successor was always going to struggle to replicate its intensity.

It’s still a good place to watch football because they are such a passionate group of supporters but the stadium is unappealing from the outside – actually it’s downright ugly – and unremarkable on the inside.

Unless, of course, it’s a South Wales derby or Bristol City are in town and then the atmosphere takes your breath away.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2002 Capacity: 25,586.

The MKM Stadium is a handsome one on the inside but there have been times I have visited when sections of it were shut down because of ticketing issues.

I’ve got a soft spot for Hull City but not for their stadium.

It is a handsome stadium on the inside but there have been times when I have visited when sections of it were shut down because of ticketing issues.

Division: Championship Opened: 1935 Capacity: 27,359.

Division: Championship Opened: 1887 Capacity: 27,000.

I’ve only been once and that was for work but Ashton Gate is a handsome stadium in a beautiful city with a rich history.

Ashton Gate is one of the stadiums that has slipped through the gaps for me.

I’ve only been once and that was for work but it’s a handsome stadium in a beautiful city with a rich history.

Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League, is a Bristol City fan, which always struck me as slightly strange given the damage the top flight did to the lower leagues during his time at the helm.

57. Memorial Stadium, Bristol Rovers.

Division: League Two Opened: 1921 Capacity: 12,500.

Owners are always threatening to move to a upcoming site but the Memorial Stadium, successor to Eastville, still survives.

A quirky mish-mash of a ground whose architecture betrays its origins as a rugby stadium, the Memorial Stadium is still a decent place to watch football.

I prefer the kind of visual chaos you get at this place – with the Popular Insulation Stand isolated like a widow stand on part of the one touchline, and the West Stand looking more like a cricket pavilion – than the monotonous uniformity you get at so many new-builds.

Owners are always threatening to move to a latest site but the Memorial Stadium, successor to Eastville, still survives.
